anchors.code: r = handle->disasm(ud, buffer, size, &mci, &insn_size, offset, handle->getinsn_info);
anchors.note: Consumes the attacker-controlled bytes `0F 1B 01` and decodes them into `mci`. The later generated-printer frame at `X86GenAsmWriter1.inc:32621` identifies the resulting internal opcode as `X86_BNDSTXmr` for this witness.

The decoded `BNDSTXmr` instruction enters generated printer case 12. That case first prints the memory operand with `printanymem(MI, 0, O)` and then, on the same `MCInst`, prints operand 5 with `printOperand(MI, 5, O)`.

Because `MI->Opcode` is `X86_BNDSTXmr`, none of the `LEA*` cases match and the switch takes the default arm. `printanymem()` therefore does not assign `MI->x86opsize`, leaving it at the indeterminate stack value from step 1.

When the memory operand finishes printing, `printMemReference()` copies the still-uninitialized `MI->x86opsize` into `MI->op1_size`. The saved MSan trace names this exact assignment as the store site where the poisoned byte is written to memory before the crash.

MSAN sink. The same `BNDSTXmr` printer case from step 3 immediately calls `printOperand(MI, 5, O)`, and this branch reads the poisoned `MI->op1_size` byte propagated in step 5. MemorySanitizer reports the use-of-uninitialized-value at this read.
